title: AI & Back-to-School Night: Anxious Parents, Nervous Teachers and Chill Coaches d-chill-coaches/
author: Conor P. Williams
summary: Conor Williams opens at a middle school back-to-school night where every classroom meets the same parental question about the school's AI policy, and teachers give rehearsed, cautious answers. He contrasts this with the gym, where nobody asks whether students may use AI to run laps. That contrast reveals his core idea: the indirect elements of school tasks matter at least as much as the direct ones. Kids run races or study chemistry and history not to retain every fact but to build goal setting, attention, persistence and confidence through difficult and often boring work. Parenting and teaching both prepare children for adulthood, and the indirect lessons matter more as adolescents gain independence. He grants that AI can help students find an error or talk through a problem, but argues that repeated shortcuts add up until the costs of skipping the academic equivalent of hill sprints become evident.
points: Parents and teachers are nervous about AI policy, and many teachers give a rehearsed answer that reflects personal concern more than school rules.
The sports analogy shows that the point of many school tasks is the indirect benefit, such as persistence and attention, not the product itself.
Learning academic content builds focus, memory and confidence through difficult and sometimes tedious study.
AI can help students find problems or talk through challenges, but each shortcut removes practice in perseverance.
The cumulative cost of skipped academic effort will become evident, as research increasingly suggests.
quotes: But it’s also because of a secret about education and child development: the indirect elements of most of the tasks we present to kids matter at least as much as the direct elements.
We have kids run those races because those help them learn how to set goals and then grind out the (often boring) work it takes to pursue them.
We hope they will build some facility with each subject, but also that they’ll develop the attention span, focus, memory, and confidence that come through difficult, sometimes tedious study.
In every class, most parents wonder it under their breath until some brave soul asks: “What’s your AI policy?
The coaches are also around on back-to-school night, but down in the gym, no one is asking if student-athletes are allowed to use AI during cross-country races.
Instead, the adults in their lives are helping them learn to persevere through complex projects, particularly the boring ones.

But as the years go on and the back-to-school nights pile up, all the shortcuts add up, until — as the research increasingly shows — the costs of skipping all those (academic) hill sprints become evident.
